write.desc: What it means for a sequence of functions to converge: pointwise convergence and the counterexamples that show its weakness, uniform convergence and how it differs in its quantifiers, and the practical and theoretical tools (sup-norm, witness points, Cauchy criterion) for deciding with proof whether a convergence is uniform.

points.name: Sequences of functions and pointwise convergence
points.what: The learner can define a sequence of functions f_n on a common domain A and its pointwise limit (for each fixed x, f_n(x) -> f(x) as a sequence of numbers), write the definition with epsilon and N, and compute pointwise limits of simple examples.
outside: epsilon-N definition of the limit of a sequence of real numbers

points.name: x^n on [0,1]: a pointwise limit that is not continuous
points.what: The learner can compute the pointwise limit of x^n on [0,1] (0 for x < 1, 1 at x = 1) and explain why this shows that a pointwise limit of continuous functions need not be continuous, phrased as two limits (in n and in x) that cannot be swapped.
outside: continuity of a function at a point

points.name: Bump sequences: integrals of the limit versus limit of integrals
points.what: The learner can work through a moving or growing bump sequence (for example a tent of height n on [0, 2/n], or n^2 x (1 - x^2)^n) that tends pointwise to 0 while its integrals do not tend to 0, and say exactly which swap of limits fails.
outside: Riemann integral of a continuous function on [a,b]

points.name: Uniform convergence: the definition
points.what: The learner can state the definition of f_n -> f uniformly on A (for every epsilon > 0 there is N with |f_n(x) - f(x)| < epsilon for all n >= N and all x in A at once), picture it as f_n lying in an epsilon-band around f, and see that uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence to the same limit.

points.name: Pointwise versus uniform: the order of quantifiers
points.what: The learner can write both definitions side by side and explain that in pointwise convergence N may depend on x (for all x, there exists N) while in uniform convergence one N must work for every x (there exists N, for all x), and can identify in an example how N depends on x.
outside: order of quantifiers in nested for-all / there-exists statements

points.name: Negating uniform convergence
points.what: The learner can correctly write the negation of uniform convergence (there is epsilon_0 > 0 such that for every N there are n >= N and x in A with |f_n(x) - f(x)| >= epsilon_0) and distinguish it from the negation of pointwise convergence.

points.name: The sup-norm view of uniform convergence
points.what: The learner can prove that f_n -> f uniformly on A exactly when sup over A of |f_n - f| tends to 0 (including the case where the sup is eventually finite), and use ||g||_inf = sup|g| with its triangle inequality as the natural way to measure the distance between functions.
outside: supremum (least upper bound) of a set of real numbers

points.name: Proving uniform convergence by bounding or computing the sup
points.what: The learner can prove a convergence is uniform by first finding the pointwise limit, then bounding sup|f_n - f| by a sequence tending to 0, or computing it exactly with calculus (for example the maximum of x/(1 + n x^2) or of x^n(1 - x) on [0,1]).
outside: finding the maximum of a differentiable function on an interval via critical points

points.name: Disproving uniform convergence with witness points
points.what: The learner can show a convergence is not uniform by exhibiting points x_n with |f_n(x_n) - f(x_n)| bounded away from 0 (for example x_n = (1/2)^(1/n) for x^n), or by noting that the sup does not tend to 0, and can recognise a discontinuous pointwise limit of continuous functions as a warning sign.

points.name: Uniform convergence on subsets
points.what: The learner can decide on which subsets a sequence converges uniformly, for example proving that x^n -> 0 uniformly on [0,b] for every b < 1 but not on [0,1), and understands that uniform convergence depends on the domain and that good behaviour on every smaller closed interval is a common pattern.

points.name: Uniform convergence does not control derivatives: sin(nx)/sqrt(n)
points.what: The learner can prove that f_n(x) = sin(nx)/sqrt(n) converges uniformly to 0 on R while the derivatives sqrt(n) cos(nx) do not converge (for example at x = 0), and concludes that differentiating a limit needs a hypothesis on the derivatives.

points.name: The Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence
points.what: The learner can state and prove that f_n converges uniformly on A if and only if it is uniformly Cauchy (for every epsilon there is N with |f_n(x) - f_m(x)| < epsilon for all n, m >= N and all x in A), using completeness to build the pointwise limit and letting m -> infinity in the inequality, and sees its use when the limit function is not known.
outside: Cauchy sequences of real numbers converge (completeness of R)
non-strict inequalities are preserved under limits of sequences
